meta.title: Operation of UV Cabinet for TLC Visualization in Pharmaceutics Laboratory

sections.purpose: To visualize TLC plates under UV light (254 nm and 365 nm) for identification, purity assessment, and quantification of pharmaceutical compounds separated by thin layer chromatography.
sections.scope: Applicable to Pharmaceutics laboratory for TLC analysis of drug substances, formulation components, and degradation products as part of pharmaceutical quality control and stability studies.
procedure: Inspect the UV cabinet for intact lamps, clean viewing window, and functional light switches.
Switch on the UV cabinet power and allow the lamps to warm up for 2 minutes before viewing.
Put on UV-protective safety goggles before switching on the UV lamps — UV radiation causes irreversible eye damage (photokeratitis).
Place the developed TLC plate in the viewing cabinet on the clean white/black platform.
For 254 nm (short-wave UV): switch on the short-wave lamp; observe spots as dark quenching zones on the bright green fluorescent background (for F254 plates).
For 365 nm (long-wave UV): switch on the long-wave lamp; observe fluorescent spots in various colours against a dark background.
Immediately mark the position of all visible spots with a pencil — UV spots are not permanent.
Determine the Rf value for each spot: Rf = Distance of spot / Distance of solvent front.
Photograph the plate under each UV wavelength using a camera or the UV cabinet camera if fitted.
For quantification: use a densitometer to scan the plate under the appropriate UV wavelength.
After UV visualization, apply derivatization spray reagents in a fume hood if additional visualization is required.
Compare observed Rf values and spot colours against the reference standard lane on the same plate.
Record: mobile phase, sample and standard identities, Rf values, and UV visualization observations in the analytical register.
Switch off all UV lamps after use; clean the cabinet interior with a damp cloth.
precautions: Always wear UV-blocking safety goggles before switching on UV lamps — do not rely on regular eyeglasses (most do not block UV).
Never look directly at the UV lamp — even brief exposure causes photokeratitis (painful eye inflammation).
Do not handle the UV lamp bulb with bare hands — skin oils cause uneven heating and premature bulb failure.
Mark spots in pencil immediately — pencil marks are not destroyed by spray reagents; ink or ball-point marks dissolve.
Replace UV lamps when output intensity drops (typically after 1000–2000 hours of use) — reduced intensity causes missed spots.
Apply spray reagents only in a fume hood — many reagents (concentrated H₂SO₄, vanillin acid) are corrosive and toxic.
Ensure the UV cabinet has adequate ventilation to dissipate ozone generated by short-wave UV lamps.
